title: Union-Find / Disjoint Set
tagline: Near-O(1) connectivity queries via union by rank and path compression — the engine behind Kruskal's MST algorithm.

sections.content:
Imagine you are maintaining a social network with millions of users. A new friendship is formed every second, and users constantly ask: "Are Alice and Bob friends — directly or through any chain of mutual friends?" A naive approach would do a graph search (BFS or DFS) for every query, taking O(V + E) time. With millions of users and billions of queries, that is catastrophically slow.

The **Union-Find** data structure — also called **Disjoint Set Union** (DSU) — was invented precisely for this scenario. It maintains a partition of n elements into disjoint (non-overlapping) sets and answers two questions with astonishing speed: **union(a, b)** merges the set containing a with the set containing b, and **find(x)** returns the canonical **representative** (or root) of the set containing x. Two elements are in the same set if and only if `find(a) === find(b)`.

With two elegant optimisations — **union by rank** and **path compression** — both operations achieve amortised **O(α(n))** time, where α is the inverse Ackermann function. This grows so slowly it is effectively constant: α(n) ≤ 4 for any n smaller than 10^600, a number vastly larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe. For all practical purposes, Union-Find gives you **O(1) connectivity queries**, no matter how many elements or merges you have.

Union-Find appears in an almost surprising breadth of real-world algorithms: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, cycle detection in undirected graphs, counting connected components, network connectivity checks, image segmentation, percolation theory, and even computer vision clustering. Understanding it deeply — not just how to code it, but *why* it works — gives you one of the most powerful tools in the algorithms toolkit.

sections.title: City Mergers and Town Representatives
sections.content:
Picture a country with thousands of small independent towns, each with its own elected representative. When two towns merge into one municipality, residents of the smaller town are told: "Whenever you need to contact your representative, go through the old representative of the larger town — they now speak for everyone."

Over time, through many mergers, some towns become part of giant cities. If you want to know whether two people live in the same city, you ask each one: "Who is your representative?" They might not know the top representative directly — they ask *their* contact, who asks theirs, tracing a chain upward until reaching the ultimate representative at the top. If both people end up at the same top-level representative, they are in the same city.

**Path compression** is the bureaucratic shortcut: the first time you trace the chain to the top, you update your records so every person along the chain gets the top representative's direct contact. Future queries skip the middlemen entirely.

**Union by rank** is the merger policy: when two cities merge, the smaller one always defers to the larger one's representative, not the other way around. This keeps chains short. If you made the larger city defer to the smaller one's representative, long chains could form — everyone in the large city would have to trace an extra hop through the small city's chain.

Together, these two policies ensure that no matter how many mergers happen, finding the representative takes essentially one phone call.

sections.title: The Core Data Structure: Parent Arrays
sections.content:
Union-Find stores one array: `parent[]`, where `parent[i]` is the parent of element i. Initially, every element is its own parent: `parent[i] = i`. This means there are n separate sets, each containing exactly one element.

The **root** (representative) of a set is the element x where `parent[x] === x` — a self-loop. To find the root of any element, you follow the parent chain: `x → parent[x] → parent[parent[x]] → …` until you reach a self-loop.

The `find` operation implements this traversal. The `union(a, b)` operation calls `find` on both elements to get their roots. If the roots are different, it sets one root's parent to the other root — merging the two trees into one.

A naive implementation with no optimisations can degenerate badly. If you always union by attaching the second root to the first, and you union elements in a chain (0-1, 1-2, 2-3, …), you build a linear chain: `n → n-1 → … → 1 → 0`. `find` on element n takes O(n) time. This is as bad as a linked list.

The two classic optimisations fix this — and together they produce near-constant time.

sections.title: Optimisation 1 — Path Compression
sections.content:
**Path compression** is applied during `find`. After tracing the chain from x all the way to the root, the algorithm sets `parent[x]` directly to the root. More powerfully, with recursive path compression, *every node along the entire path* is pointed directly to the root in a single traversal.

The code is elegant: `find(x)` is implemented as a one-liner that calls itself recursively and assigns the result back before returning:

```
if (parent[x] !== x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]);
return parent[x];
```

Here is how the recursion works: `find(parent[x])` recurses all the way up to the root, then on the way *back* (during stack unwinding), it assigns `parent[x] = root` for every x along the path. The result is a fully flattened tree — every node on the path becomes a direct child of the root.

After path compression, future `find` calls on those same nodes take exactly **one hop**: node → root. This amortises the cost: you pay O(depth) once and O(1) for every subsequent query on the same nodes.

A variant called **path splitting** (or path halving) makes each node point to its grandparent instead of the root. It achieves the same asymptotic complexity but is iterative, avoiding recursion stack overhead.

sections.title: Optimisation 2 — Union by Rank (and Union by Size)
sections.content:
**Union by rank** prevents the tree from growing unnecessarily tall during merges. Each root maintains a `rank` value — an upper bound on the height of its subtree. When unioning two trees:

- If `rank[rootA] < rank[rootB]`: attach rootA under rootB. The taller tree stays as root.
- If `rank[rootA] > rank[rootB]`: attach rootB under rootA.
- If `rank[rootA] === rank[rootB]`: either can become the root, but the winner's rank **increments by 1**.

Why does rank only increment when ranks are equal? Consider two trees both of height h. Merging them creates a tree of height h+1 at most. If one has height h and the other has height h-1, the combined tree still has height h — unchanged. So rank only increases when two equal-height trees combine.

Without path compression but with union by rank, tree height is bounded by **O(log n)**. This alone gives O(log n) per operation — already much better than O(n).

An alternative to rank is **union by size**: always attach the smaller set under the larger one, tracking the exact element count. Union by size gives the same O(log n) bound and makes it easy to query set sizes. When path compression is also applied, both strategies achieve O(α(n)) amortised.

A subtle but important point: after path compression, `rank` values can become inaccurate (they are upper bounds, not exact heights). This is fine — the algorithm still works correctly because rank is only used to decide which root to attach, not to measure the actual depth.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The class tracks both `rank` (for merge decisions) and `size` (for set cardinality queries). Path compression is the single recursive line that rewrites `parent[x]` to the ultimate root during the call stack unwind. `union` returns `false` when roots are equal — this boolean is the cycle-detection signal used by Kruskal's algorithm.

sections.title: Why O(α(n))? The Inverse Ackermann Function
sections.content:
The amortised complexity of Union-Find with both optimisations is **O(α(n)) per operation**, where α is the **inverse Ackermann function**. This deserves explanation because it is one of the most interesting complexity results in computer science.

The Ackermann function A(m, n) grows extraordinarily fast — faster than any primitive recursive function. Its inverse, α(n), therefore grows extraordinarily slowly. Concretely:
- α(n) = 1 for n ≤ 1
- α(n) = 2 for n ≤ 4
- α(n) = 3 for n ≤ 2^65536
- α(n) = 4 for n ≤ A(4, ...) — a number with 2^65536 digits
- α(n) = 5 for n smaller than something unimaginably large

For any n you could ever encounter in a program — or in fact in the physical universe — **α(n) ≤ 4**. In every real-world use of Union-Find, each operation takes at most 4 levels of traversal on average. Practitioners call this "effectively O(1)" and that is not an exaggeration.

This result was proved by Robert Tarjan in 1975 and later tightened by Tarjan and Jan van Leeuwen. Proving that Union-Find operations are *not* O(1) in the strict sense (i.e., that α(n) is actually necessary and not just an artifact of the proof technique) is a non-trivial lower-bound result. The true complexity lies in a narrow band between O(1) and O(log* n) — and it is exactly O(α(n)).

For interview and practical purposes: just say "near-constant" or "essentially O(1)" and know that the formal name is O(α(n)).

sections.title: Key Application — Cycle Detection in Undirected Graphs
sections.content:
One of Union-Find's most common interview applications is detecting cycles in an undirected graph. The idea is beautifully simple:

1. Initialise Union-Find with n nodes.
2. For each edge (u, v), call `find(u)` and `find(v)`.
3. If they return the **same root**, u and v are already connected — adding this edge would create a cycle.
4. If they return **different roots**, call `union(u, v)` to merge their sets.

After processing all edges without finding a cycle, the graph is acyclic. This approach is O(E α(V)) — essentially O(E) — far better than running DFS for each edge at O(E × (V + E)).

**Important caveat**: this only works for **undirected** graphs. In a directed graph, Union-Find cannot distinguish between a directed path A→B→C and its reverse. Directed cycle detection requires DFS with a recursion-stack (three-color marking: white/gray/black) to detect back edges.

sections.title: Key Application — Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree
sections.content:
A **minimum spanning tree** (MST) of a weighted undirected graph is a subset of edges that connects all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight and no cycles. An MST has exactly V-1 edges for a graph with V vertices.

**Kruskal's algorithm** is a greedy approach that builds the MST edge by edge:
1. Sort all edges by weight (ascending).
2. Process edges in order. For each edge (u, v, weight):
   - If u and v are in **different components** (`!uf.connected(u, v)`), adding this edge is safe — include it in the MST and call `union(u, v)`.
   - If they are in the **same component** (`uf.connected(u, v)`), skip this edge — including it would create a cycle.
3. Stop when the MST has V-1 edges (or all edges are exhausted).

Union-Find is the critical sub-routine here. Without it, checking whether adding an edge creates a cycle would require running BFS or DFS from scratch — O(V + E) per edge, totalling O(E(V + E)) for the whole algorithm. With Union-Find, each connectivity check and merge is O(α(V)), so the total complexity is **O(E log E)** dominated by the initial sort.

Kruskal's algorithm is correct because of the **cut property** of MSTs: for any cut of the graph (partition of vertices into two groups), the cheapest edge crossing the cut must be in some MST. By processing edges in order and only adding safe ones, Kruskal greedily picks the cheapest valid edge at every step.

flowchart LR
  A["Sort edges\nby weight"] --> B["Take next\ncheapest edge\n(u, v, w)"]
  B --> C{"find(u)\n=== find(v)?"}
  C -- "Yes\n(cycle!)" --> D["Skip edge"]
  C -- "No\n(safe)" --> E["union(u, v)\nAdd to MST"]
  D --> F{"MST has\nV-1 edges?"}
  E --> F
  F -- "No" --> B
  F -- "Yes" --> G["MST complete"]
sections.caption: Kruskal's algorithm loop: sort once, then for each edge use Union-Find to check for cycles in O(α(V)) time. The sort is the bottleneck at O(E log E).

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: hasCycle processes edges one by one; if union returns false (already connected), a cycle exists. kruskalMST sorts first then greedily adds safe edges. The check `uf.count() === 1` after the loop tells you if the graph was connected — a disconnected graph yields a spanning forest, not a spanning tree.

sections.title: Other Applications and Variants
sections.content:
Union-Find appears in more places than most developers expect:

**Counting connected components**: After processing all edges, `uf.count()` gives the number of connected components. This is exactly what LeetCode "Number of Islands" uses — treat each land cell as a node, union adjacent land cells, and count components.

**Percolation simulation**: In physics and materials science, percolation asks whether a material conducts electricity end-to-end. Model each cell as a node, union adjacent open cells, and ask whether the top and bottom rows share a root. This is a famous application studied by computational physicists.

**Image segmentation**: In computer vision, pixels are nodes. Union adjacent pixels whose colours are similar. The resulting components are image regions. This underpins simple flood-fill algorithms and some cluster-based segmentation approaches.

**Offline LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor)**: Tarjan's offline LCA algorithm uses Union-Find to answer all LCA queries in a single DFS pass.

**Dynamic connectivity**: More advanced variants of Union-Find support "link" (union) and "cut" (split a set back apart) operations, though cut makes things significantly more complex — this is the domain of link-cut trees, a much harder data structure.

**Weighted Union-Find**: Some problems require tracking a relationship between elements and their root — for example, the difference or ratio between an element's value and the root's value. This is done by storing a `weight` array alongside the parent array and propagating weights during path compression and union. LeetCode 399 (Evaluate Division) uses this pattern.

sections.title: Common Mistakes and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Forgetting to call find before union**: A common bug is calling `union(parent[a], parent[b])` instead of `union(find(a), find(b))`. Always use `find` to get the roots — attaching non-root nodes directly creates an incorrect tree structure.

**Union on directed graphs**: Union-Find is symmetric — `union(a, b)` is the same as `union(b, a)`. It cannot encode the direction of a relationship. Applying it to directed graphs gives wrong answers for directed cycle detection.

**Off-by-one errors in initialisation**: If nodes are 1-indexed (as in many competitive programming problems), initialise the parent array with size n+1 or map indices down by 1. Accessing `parent[0]` when nodes start at 1 is a silent bug.

**Relying on rank as exact height**: After path compression, `rank[x]` is no longer the exact height of the subtree rooted at x — it is an upper bound. Never use rank values to answer questions about actual tree structure.

**Using union-find for directed connectivity**: If your problem has directed edges and you need reachability ("can I get from A to B following edge directions?"), Union-Find gives wrong answers. Use DFS/BFS or Tarjan's SCC algorithm.

**Stack overflow with deep trees**: The recursive `find` implementation can hit JavaScript/Python stack limits on pathological inputs (before path compression kicks in). If n is very large or you are not sure about the input order, use the iterative version.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The iterative path-splitting find avoids recursion entirely and is safe for very deep trees. The weighted variant stores a multiplicative relationship between each node and its root, updated during path compression by chaining the weights. This is the core technique for LeetCode 399 (Evaluate Division).

sections.content: **Historical context:** The Union-Find problem was studied as early as 1964 by Bernard Galler and Michael Fisher, who published the first union by rank variant. Path compression was described independently by several researchers in the late 1960s. Robert Tarjan proved the O(log* n) bound in 1975, then with van Leeuwen proved the tight O(α(n)) bound in 1984. The result that O(α(n)) is also a *lower bound* — that no algorithm can do better — was proved by Fredman and Saks in 1989. This makes Union-Find one of the rare data structures where we know its exact complexity, and that complexity happens to be this fascinating near-constant function.

**Interview insights and common traps:**
- When a graph problem asks about connected components, cycles, or connectivity in an *undirected* graph, Union-Find is almost always the cleanest solution.
- The return value of `union(a, b)` — `false` when already connected — is a built-in cycle detector. Use it directly in Kruskal's MST without a separate `connected` check.
- For grid problems (islands, percolation), flatten 2D coordinates: node index = `row * cols + col`. This avoids building an explicit adjacency list.
- Initialise `components = n` and decrement on each successful union. After all unions, `components` is the answer to "how many connected components are there?" — no extra traversal needed.
- If asked about directed graphs, Union-Find gives wrong cycle detection. Always clarify edge directionality before reaching for DSU.
- `union by size` (tracking element counts) is often more useful than `union by rank` for problems that also need set cardinality — the complexity is identical.

items: **Union-Find (DSU)** maintains a partition of n elements into disjoint sets and supports two operations: `find(x)` returns the root of x's set, and `union(a, b)` merges two sets. Two elements are connected if and only if `find(a) === find(b)`.

**Path compression** (setting every node on the find path directly to the root) and **union by rank** (always attaching the smaller tree under the larger) together achieve amortised **O(α(n))** per operation — effectively O(1) for all practical inputs.
The **inverse Ackermann function α(n)** grows so slowly that α(n) ≤ 4 for any n in the observable universe. Neither optimisation alone achieves this; both are required together to reach O(α(n)).

**Cycle detection**: before calling `union(u, v)`, check `connected(u, v)`. If true, the edge creates a cycle. This works only for *undirected* graphs — use DFS with color-marking for directed graphs.
**Kruskal's MST** sorts edges by weight, then greedily adds each edge if it does not create a cycle (verified by Union-Find in O(α(V))). Total complexity is **O(E log E)** dominated by the sort.

Union-Find answers *only* the yes/no connectivity question. It cannot answer 'what is the path?' or 'list all members of a set?' — for those, use BFS/DFS or store extra data structures alongside the DSU.

Advanced variants include **weighted DSU** (tracking ratios between elements and their roots), useful for currency conversion and equation evaluation problems, and **union by size** (tracking set cardinalities), useful when you need to know how large each component is.

quiz.question: What does `find(x)` return in a Union-Find data structure?
options: The index of x in the parent array
The root (representative) of the set containing x
The rank of x
The size of the set containing x
quiz.explanation: find(x) follows the parent chain from x until it reaches a node that is its own parent (a self-loop). That node is the root — the canonical representative of x's set. Two elements share a set if and only if their roots are equal.

quiz.question: What does path compression accomplish during a `find` call?
options: It sorts the elements within a set by value to speed future lookups
It points every node traversed on the find path directly to the root, flattening the tree
It splits a large set into two balanced sub-trees to maintain O(log n) height
It removes intermediate nodes from the set to reduce memory usage
quiz.explanation: After find(x) recursively reaches the root, the call stack unwinds and sets parent[x] = root for every node x along the path. This flattens the entire traversed chain so future find calls on those nodes take a single hop. It is the single most impactful optimisation in Union-Find.

quiz.question: What does the `rank` value of a root node represent, and when does it increment?
options: The exact count of elements in the set; it increments on every successful union
An upper bound on the subtree height; it increments only when two roots of equal rank are merged
The order in which the root was first created; it never changes
The depth of the deepest leaf; it increments whenever path compression runs
quiz.explanation: Rank is an upper bound on tree height (it can become inaccurate after path compression but remains useful for merge decisions). When merging two trees of equal rank, the resulting tree is one level taller, so the winner's rank increments. When ranks differ, the shorter tree attaches under the taller one and the taller root's rank is unchanged.

quiz.question: How does Union-Find detect a cycle when building an undirected graph edge by edge?
options: By counting the total number of union operations performed and comparing to V-1
By checking whether both endpoints of the new edge already share the same root before calling union
By running a full DFS after each edge insertion to look for back edges
By comparing the ranks of the two endpoint nodes — equal ranks signal a cycle
quiz.explanation: Before calling union(u, v), check if find(u) === find(v). If they share a root, u and v are already in the same connected component — adding this edge creates a cycle. If their roots differ, the edge is safe; call union to merge the components. This is exactly the test Kruskal's MST algorithm uses.

quiz.question: What is the amortised per-operation time complexity of Union-Find with BOTH path compression and union by rank?
options: O(1) exact in all cases
O(log n) per operation
O(α(n)) — inverse Ackermann, effectively constant for all practical inputs
O(log log n) per operation
quiz.explanation: With both optimisations applied together, the amortised cost per operation is O(α(n)) where α is the inverse Ackermann function. α(n) ≤ 4 for any n smaller than a number with 10^19728 digits — effectively constant. Applying only one optimisation gives O(log n); neither alone achieves O(α(n)).

quiz.question: In Kruskal's MST algorithm, why is Union-Find preferred over running BFS to check for cycles?
options: BFS cannot handle weighted edges, so it gives wrong MST results
Union-Find cycle checks are near-O(1) per edge versus O(V+E) per BFS, reducing total complexity from O(E(V+E)) to O(E log E)
BFS only detects cycles in directed graphs, not undirected ones
Union-Find guarantees the MST is unique, whereas BFS might select arbitrary edges
quiz.explanation: Kruskal processes every edge once. A BFS cycle check is O(V+E) per edge, giving O(E(V+E)) total — unacceptably slow. Union-Find reduces each check to O(α(V)), so the E cycle checks cost O(Eα(V)) total. The algorithm becomes O(E log E) dominated by the initial sort — a dramatic improvement.

quiz.question: When union(a, b) is called and a and b are already in the same set, what should happen?
options: The component count decrements by 1 anyway, to record the duplicate edge
The component count increments by 1, since a new edge was added
No merge occurs — the component count stays the same, and the call returns false to signal a cycle
The entire set is reset and both elements become singletons
quiz.explanation: If find(a) === find(b), both elements are already in the same component. No structural change is needed — the parent array and component count remain unchanged. A well-implemented union returns false in this case, which directly serves as the cycle-detection signal in Kruskal's algorithm.

quiz.question: Can Union-Find be used directly to detect cycles in a **directed** graph?
options: Yes — union and find work identically regardless of edge direction
No — Union-Find is undirected; directed cycle detection requires DFS with a recursion-stack or three-color marking
Yes, but only if you process edges in topological sort order
No — Union-Find can only detect self-loops, not cycles of length 2 or more
quiz.explanation: Union-Find treats every edge as bidirectional. In a directed graph, A→B does not imply B→A, but Union-Find would union them symmetrically. A directed cycle like A→B→C→A would be detected, but so would A→B, C→B treated as A-B-C, giving false positives. Use DFS with GRAY/WHITE/BLACK coloring to detect directed back edges properly.

quiz.question: After exactly n-1 successful `union` calls on n initially separate elements, what is the component count?
options: n — one component per element, unchanged
n-1 — one component was skipped
1 — all elements are now in a single connected component
0 — the component count underflows to zero
quiz.explanation: Starting with n components (each element is its own set), each *successful* union (where the two elements were in different sets) reduces the count by exactly 1. After n-1 successful merges, the count reaches 1 — one set containing all elements. This is the structure of a spanning tree on n vertices.

quiz.question: Which of the following problems is Union-Find LEAST suited to solve efficiently?
options: Counting the number of connected components in an undirected graph
Finding the shortest path between two nodes in a weighted graph
Detecting whether adding an edge to an undirected graph creates a cycle
Determining whether two nodes are in the same connected component
quiz.explanation: Union-Find answers only yes/no connectivity — it records which set an element belongs to but does not store the actual path or edge sequence. Finding the shortest path requires BFS (unweighted) or Dijkstra's algorithm (weighted), which track the actual traversal structure. Union-Find excels at the other three: component counting, cycle detection, and connectivity queries.
